title: A4 — Cost-optimized storage
bodyMarkdown:
## Cost-optimized storage

Exam task **4.1**. Lessons 2.2, 3.1, and 3.5 already covered S3 durability, EBS volume types, EFS performance modes, FSx, DataSync, Storage Gateway, and columnar formats — this lesson does not repeat those mechanics. It applies the same services through a **cost** lens: which storage class, tier, tool, or lifecycle rule lowers spend for a stated access pattern, retention period, or budget constraint.

### K01 — Access options (for example, an S3 bucket with Requester Pays object storage)

By default the bucket owner pays for both storage and every request or data transfer against a bucket. **Requester Pays** flips that: the account making the request pays for the request and any data downloaded, while the owner still pays only for storage. Turning Requester Pays on disables anonymous access — every request must be authenticated and must include the `x-amz-request-payer` header (or the CLI `--request-payer` flag) so AWS can bill the correct account; a request that omits it is rejected. This fits a bucket that shares large public datasets (reference data, geospatial extracts, web-crawl corpora) where the owner wants to publish the data without absorbing everyone else's download costs.

**Exam tip:** "share a large dataset publicly without paying for other people's downloads" is Requester Pays; the owner keeps paying for storage regardless.

### K02 — AWS cost management service features (for example, cost allocation tags, multi-account billing)

**Cost allocation tags** let Billing and Cost Management break spend down by team, project, or environment; both AWS-generated and user-defined tags must be activated in the Billing console before they appear as columns in Cost Explorer or the Cost and Usage Report — tagging a resource alone is not enough. **Consolidated (multi-account) billing** under AWS Organizations rolls every member account's usage into one payer account, combining usage to reach volume pricing tiers and sharing the benefit of Reserved Instances and Savings Plans purchased by any account in the organization. **AWS Billing Conductor** builds on consolidated billing to model custom, chargeback-style rates per account or business unit without changing what AWS actually charges.

**Exam tip:** an untagged resource, or a tag that was never activated, never shows up in a cost report — activation is a separate step from tagging.

### K03 — AWS cost management tools with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, AWS Cost and Usage Report)

**AWS Cost Explorer** visualizes and forecasts cost and usage with built-in and custom reports, filtered by service, linked account, or tag — the go-to tool for "why did the bill change" or "what will next quarter cost." **AWS Budgets** does not report history; it watches actual or forecasted cost or usage against a threshold and alerts (email or SNS) when breached, including Reserved Instance or Savings Plans utilization and coverage alerts. The **AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR)**, alongside the newer **Data Exports**, delivers the most granular line-item billing data, dropped into an S3 bucket for direct query with Athena or a BI tool — use it when Cost Explorer's aggregated view isn't granular enough.

**Exam tip:** "visualize and forecast" is Cost Explorer; "alert me before I overspend" is Budgets; "every line item, queryable" is the CUR or Data Exports.

### K04 — AWS storage services with appropriate use cases (for example, Amazon FSx, Amazon EFS, Amazon S3, Amazon EBS)

Lessons 2.2 and 3.1 covered what each service does; the cost distinction is how each bills. **Amazon S3** bills only for what you store, by storage class, plus requests and retrievals — no capacity to provision, so it is normally cheapest for object data at scale. **Amazon EFS** also bills per GB actually stored with no pre-provisioned capacity, but its per-GB rate is higher than S3's. **Amazon EBS** bills for provisioned size, and for io1/io2/gp3, provisioned IOPS and throughput — you pay for what you provisioned whether or not you use it, so idle or oversized volumes are pure waste. **FSx** prices for a managed, purpose-built engine (Lustre, Windows File Server, ONTAP, OpenZFS) and is usually the most expensive of the four; reserve it for workloads that specifically need that engine's protocol or feature set.

**Exam tip:** "pay only for what's stored, no provisioning" points to S3 or EFS; "pay for what you provisioned" points to EBS or FSx.

### K05 — Backup strategies

A backup strategy balances recovery objectives against storage cost. **AWS Backup** centralizes policy-driven backup across many AWS resource types: after the first, full backup, most supported resources back up incrementally, so ongoing storage cost reflects only the changed data. A backup plan's lifecycle can transition older recovery points to a **cold storage tier** automatically; once moved, a recovery point must stay in cold storage at least 90 days (in addition to any time already spent in warm storage) before it can be deleted or restored back to warm storage. Snapshot-based strategies for individual services (EBS snapshots, RDS snapshots) work without AWS Backup but require you to script cross-service consistency and retention yourself.

**Exam tip:** "one policy, many services, incremental after the first copy" is AWS Backup; a recovery point moved to cold storage is locked in for 90 days minimum.

### K06 — Block storage options (for example, hard disk drive [HDD] volume types, solid state drive [SSD] volume types)

Lesson 3.1 covered EBS volume type performance; for cost, **gp3** is the newer and cheaper general-purpose SSD — about 20% lower price per GiB than **gp2** at equivalent performance, because gp3 provisions IOPS and throughput independently of size instead of forcing a larger volume for more baseline IOPS. **io1/io2** price per provisioned IOPS on top of per-GiB storage, a premium worth paying only when a workload genuinely needs guaranteed high IOPS at low latency. The HDD types, **st1** and **sc1**, price by throughput rather than IOPS and cost less per GiB than any SSD; **sc1** is the cheapest EBS type of all, fitting cold, infrequent, sequential data that gp3 or st1 would over-serve.

**Exam tip:** migrating idle gp2 volumes to gp3 is a same-performance cost cut; sc1 is the answer whenever a stem says "coldest, cheapest, sequential, infrequent."

### K07 — Data lifecycles

A data lifecycle is the sequence of access states data passes through over time — frequently accessed, then infrequently accessed, then archival, then deleted — and cost optimization means matching storage to the current state instead of leaving everything on its most expensive tier forever. AWS expresses this as policy in several places: **S3 Lifecycle** rules for objects, **EFS Lifecycle Management** for files, the **EBS Snapshot Archive** tier for snapshots, and **AWS Backup lifecycle** settings for recovery points. All four share the same shape: a number of days since creation or last access triggers a transition or an expiration, so nobody has to move or delete data by hand.

**Exam tip:** any stem describing data that "gets colder over time" is asking you to name the lifecycle policy for that resource type, not to design a manual process.

### K08 — Hybrid storage options (for example, AWS DataSync, AWS Transfer Family, AWS Storage Gateway)

Storage Gateway's three gateway types (lesson 3.1) reduce on-premises hardware spend by keeping only a cache locally and the bulk of data in AWS. **AWS DataSync** charges per GB transferred with no gateway appliance to run, making it the lower-cost choice for a bulk, one-time, or recurring online migration or replication job between on-premises storage (or another cloud) and S3, EFS, or FSx. **AWS Transfer Family** is different again: it provides managed SFTP, FTPS, AS2, and FTP endpoints backed by S3 or EFS, priced per protocol endpoint-hour plus data transfer, for exchanging files with external partners who require one of those legacy protocols — without standing up and patching EC2-hosted FTP servers yourself.

**Exam tip:** "external partner needs SFTP" is Transfer Family; "move or sync a bulk dataset into AWS storage" is DataSync; "keep serving on-premises apps from a local cache backed by AWS" is Storage Gateway.

### K09 — Storage access patterns

An access pattern is how often, how predictably, and how quickly data must be retrieved, and it is the single input that drives almost every storage-tier decision in this lesson. Frequent, unpredictable access belongs on a class with no retrieval fee (S3 Standard, EFS Standard); frequent but well-understood infrequent access can be tiered manually to save the monitoring fee that automatic tiering charges; access that is rare but must still complete in milliseconds needs an instant-retrieval class; access that can tolerate minutes-to-hours of retrieval time can move to an archival class for the lowest storage cost.

**Exam tip:** when a stem states how often and how fast data must be retrieved, it is telling you exactly which storage class or tier to pick — treat the access-pattern language as the deciding fact, not the data type.

### K10 — Storage tiering (for example, cold tiering for object storage)

Cold tiering moves data that is no longer hot into a class priced for infrequent or archival access. For S3 objects that means **Standard-IA**, **One Zone-IA**, **Glacier Instant Retrieval**, **Glacier Flexible Retrieval**, and **Glacier Deep Archive**, in increasing order of coldness and decreasing storage cost. Every class below Standard carries a minimum storage duration before you can delete, overwrite, or transition out without an early charge: 30 days for the two IA classes, 90 days for Glacier Instant and Flexible Retrieval, 180 days for Deep Archive — plus, for the IA classes and Glacier Instant Retrieval, a 128 KB minimum billed object size. **S3 Storage Lens** gives organization-wide visibility into buckets missing lifecycle rules or holding data that should be tiered, with a free metrics tier and a paid advanced tier for deeper analysis. Block and file storage have their own cold tiers too: the EBS Snapshot Archive tier and the EFS Archive storage class.

**Exam tip:** cold tiering saves the most for data that will genuinely sit past its class's minimum duration; moving data out early converts the promised savings into an early-deletion or early-transition charge.

### K11 — Storage types with associated characteristics (for example, object, file, block)

The three storage types price differently because they solve different problems. **Object storage (S3)** has no capacity to provision and needs no minimum object size or duration for its default Standard class — you pay per GB stored plus requests, and **S3 Express One Zone** prices requests about 50% lower than Standard in exchange for single-AZ redundancy. **Block storage (EBS)** must be sized (and for io1/io2/gp3, provisioned for IOPS and throughput) in advance, and that capacity bills whether or not it is used — an unattached or oversized volume is pure waste, so deleting or downsizing unattached volumes is a standing cost-optimization task. **File storage (EFS, FSx)** falls in between: EFS grows and shrinks with usage like S3, while FSx requires provisioning storage (and, for some deployment types, throughput) similarly to EBS.

**Exam tip:** "billed for provisioned capacity regardless of use" describes EBS (and FSx); "billed only for what's actually stored" describes S3 and EFS.

### S01 — Designing appropriate storage strategies (for example, batch uploads to Amazon S3 compared with individual uploads)

Every S3 PUT, COPY, POST, and DELETE request is billed per request, so a workload that uploads one object at a time for thousands of small records pays far more in request charges than the same data grouped into fewer, larger objects, or delivered through **S3 Batch Operations** for large-scale copy or tagging jobs. For a single large object, split the upload into parts with **multipart upload** so parts transfer in parallel and a failed part only needs to be retried, not the whole object — and remember that incomplete multipart uploads still bill for the storage they hold until an S3 Lifecycle rule expires them.

**Exam tip:** "many small objects or records to upload" favors batching or Batch Operations over one request per record; always pair multipart upload with a lifecycle rule that expires incomplete uploads.

### S02 — Determining the correct storage size for a workload

Because EBS bills provisioned size (and, for io1/io2/gp3, provisioned IOPS and throughput) whether or not it's used, sizing a volume to actual measured need — rather than guessing high "to be safe" — is a direct cost lever. **Elastic Volumes** let you grow size, change type, or adjust performance later without downtime, so the safer strategy is to start at a realistic size and scale up when metrics justify it rather than over-provisioning up front. S3, EFS, and FSx with elastic throughput remove this decision for storage capacity entirely, since they bill actual usage — the sizing question there is about performance settings (EFS throughput mode, FSx deployment type), not capacity.

**Exam tip:** "avoid paying for unused provisioned capacity" is an EBS Elastic Volumes answer, not a reason to move the workload to a different service.

### S03 — Determining the lowest cost method of transferring data for a workload to AWS storage

Moving data into AWS storage classes has no separate ingress charge — the only cost to compare is the transfer method's own service fee. For an ongoing or bulk transfer over an existing network link, **AWS DataSync** is normally the lowest-cost method: it is billed per GB transferred with no appliance to provision, and it can saturate the available bandwidth without custom scripts. For a dataset far too large for the available network within an acceptable time, the current low-cost path is **AWS Data Transfer Terminal**, a physical high-speed facility — the Snow Family of shippable devices it replaced is closed to new customers. For a small, occasional set of objects, a direct S3 upload (console, CLI, or SDK) has no separate service fee at all.

**Exam tip:** "recurring, over the network, verified transfer" is DataSync; "far too much data for the network, even overnight" is Data Transfer Terminal, never the retired Snowball Edge.

### S04 — Determining when storage auto scaling is required

**S3** and **EFS** already scale storage capacity automatically with no size to provision and nothing to design — there is no "auto scaling" decision to make for their storage capacity. **EBS** volumes do not auto-scale: a volume stays at its provisioned size and performance until you resize it with Elastic Volumes, whether manually or through automation you build (for example, a CloudWatch alarm triggering a Lambda function). **FSx** file systems similarly need capacity increases requested explicitly on most deployment types. So "storage auto scaling is required" really means EBS- or FSx-backed storage that must grow unattended — S3 and EFS never raise that problem.

**Exam tip:** if a stem worries about a volume filling up unattended, it is describing EBS (build the automation) — S3 and EFS need no such design at all.

### S05 — Managing S3 object lifecycles

An S3 Lifecycle configuration combines **transition actions** (move an object to a cheaper class after N days) and **expiration actions** (delete the current version, noncurrent versions, delete markers, or incomplete multipart uploads after N days). Transitions must follow S3's supported waterfall order, and a rule cannot schedule a transition that would complete before an earlier class's minimum storage duration has elapsed; by default only objects of at least 128 KB transition, though a rule can add an object-size filter to include smaller ones. A very common cost-saving rule that many buckets miss: expire incomplete multipart uploads after a set number of days, since S3 still bills for those unfinished parts as storage.

**Exam tip:** "objects keep failing to transition" in a stem featuring small objects points to the 128 KB default floor, not a broken rule.

### S06 — Selecting the appropriate backup and/or archival solution

Choose **AWS Backup** when the requirement spans multiple resource types (EBS, EFS, RDS, DynamoDB, and more) under one retention and compliance policy — it backs up incrementally after the first copy and can automatically age recovery points into its cold storage tier. Choose a service-native snapshot (an EBS snapshot moved to the **EBS Snapshot Archive tier**) when the requirement is EBS-only long-term retention without needing AWS Backup's cross-service policy engine — archiving offers up to about 75% lower storage cost for snapshots kept 90 days or longer that are rarely accessed. Choose direct **S3 Glacier** storage classes when the data being archived is already object data rather than a resource snapshot.

**Exam tip:** "one policy across many AWS resource types" is AWS Backup; "just this EBS volume's history, cheaply, for a long time" is the EBS Snapshot Archive tier.

### S07 — Selecting the appropriate service for data migration to storage services

Match the service to the data's source and how long the migration will run. A one-time or recurring bulk copy from an on-premises NFS/SMB share, HDFS cluster, or another cloud's object store into S3, EFS, or FSx is **AWS DataSync**'s job. A requirement to keep serving on-premises applications from AWS storage indefinitely, rather than complete a cutover, calls for **Storage Gateway** instead — that is hybrid access, not a migration you finish and turn off. External partners delivering or retrieving files over SFTP, FTPS, or AS2 belong on **AWS Transfer Family**, not a general-purpose migration tool.

**Exam tip:** "finish the migration and disconnect" is DataSync; "keep the on-premises app running against AWS storage" is Storage Gateway; "an outside partner's file protocol" is Transfer Family.

### S08 — Selecting the appropriate storage tier

Combine the access pattern (K09) with the retrieval-time tolerance and the minimum-duration commitment (K10) to land on one tier per requirement: known, frequent access stays on the default (S3 Standard, EFS Standard, gp3); known, infrequent-but-millisecond access moves to an IA or Glacier Instant Retrieval class; unpredictable or changing access moves to S3 Intelligent-Tiering, which carries no retrieval fee in exchange for a small monitoring fee; and true archival data that can wait minutes to hours moves to Glacier Flexible Retrieval or, for annual-or-rarer access, Glacier Deep Archive.

**Exam tip:** "access pattern is unknown or changes" is always Intelligent-Tiering — picking a fixed IA or Glacier class for unpredictable data risks retrieval fees or early-deletion charges.

### S09 — Selecting the correct data lifecycle for storage

Design the lifecycle as a concrete schedule of transitions and an eventual expiration, expressed as the days-since-creation-or-last-access numbers a Lifecycle or EFS Lifecycle Management policy needs — for example, Standard for 30 days, then Standard-IA, then Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 90 days, then Glacier Deep Archive at 180 days, then expire at a stated retention limit. Respect each class's minimum storage duration when spacing the transitions, since scheduling one earlier than the minimum still bills for the shortfall. Apply the same discipline to EBS snapshots (schedule the move to the Snapshot Archive tier) and to AWS Backup recovery points (set the lifecycle's cold-storage transition day count) rather than leaving retention manual.

**Exam tip:** a lifecycle "selected" for an exam scenario is a specific day-count schedule matched to the stated retention and access requirement, not just a class name.

### S10 — Selecting the most cost-effective storage service for a workload

Bring K04, K11, and the access pattern together: a data lake or static content workload with no need for a POSIX file interface belongs on S3 with a lifecycle policy, the cheapest baseline. Shared, POSIX-compliant file access with unpredictable growth belongs on EFS, whose per-GB rate is higher than S3 but needs no capacity planning and can tier to EFS-IA or EFS-Archive. A requirement that specifically needs Windows/AD-native SMB, an HPC Lustre file system, or NetApp ONTAP features justifies FSx's premium, because no cheaper service meets that requirement. A single-instance database or boot volume needing guaranteed low-latency block access is EBS, sized and typed (K06) to the actual, not the imagined, performance need.

**Exam tip:** start from "does this need a POSIX file interface or a specific vendor engine" — if not, S3 is almost always the cheapest correct answer.

### Warnings

- Do not use the AWS root user for routine lab work.
- Stopping an instance is not teardown.
- $10 budget alerts warn; they do not stop spend.
